newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - S.African Nov reserves seen up, PPI rises.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - S.African Nov reserves seen up, PPI rises.

text.p: South Africa's precariously low official reserves of gold and foreign exchange will end November slightly up from a month ago, helped by renewed inflows on the back of a firmer rand, economists said on Friday.

However, a weak rand gold price will offset some of the gain on the forex side, leaving the total end-month figure at 10.38 billion rand, marginally up from 10.28 billion in October, according to a Reuters consensus poll.
Individual forecasts for end-November reserves, due out next Friday, ranged between 10.0 billion and 11.0 billion rand.
The rand has staged a strong run following last week's one-point hike in interest rates, encouraging foreigners back into the bond market in particular.
"We've seen a good inflow of funds in the past week or so with the appreciation of the rand," said Henry Flint, economist at stockbroker Mathison and Hollidge.

But the gold element of reserves will have been hit by a fall in the the dollar bullion price and the appreciation of the rand itself, which deflates the rand value of gold holdings, said Magan Mistry of Nedcor.
Gold accounted for 60 percent of total reserves at the end of October.
Reserves of around 10.4 billion rand represent just over four weeks import cover.
Other important indicators due next week include producer price inflation (PPI) and third quarter current account figures, both scheduled for release on Thursday.
PPI is expected to move higher to a year-on-year 7.9 percent following a similar upward move in October consumer price inflation to a 16-month high of 9.1 percent.
Many economists were baffled by the low rate of increase in PPI in September, and in particular the failure of the figures to reflect higher rand oil prices.
That higher oil price is now expected to feed through in October with economists expecting a fairly hefty month-on-month increase in PPI of 1.0 percent after September's surpisingly low 0.4 percent.

The current account details will be released in the Reserve Bank's Quarterly Bulletin on Thursday. But the figures should not surprise since Bank Governor Chris Stals has already signalled a strong improvement in the figures.

Stals said at the time of last week's Bank rate hike that preliminary estimates indicated a seasonally adjusted and annualised third quarter current account deficit of about 10 billion rand against 16.4 billion in the second quarter.
Next week will also see the release of much-delayed trade figures for October on Monday, with analysts looking for a surplus of 900 million rand, up from 670 million in September.
